questions.q: In the poem "एक दिन एक दिन दौँका", who is the primary speaker (protagonist) and what collective identity do they represent?
questions.a: The primary speaker is the collective "we" (गे), representing daily-wage laborers who work from dawn to dusk. A wrong answer (e.g., identifying the poet as the speaker) reveals the student confuses the poet with the persona and misses the collective voice essential to protest poetry.

questions.q: The poem mentions "lc ?kfV varfj rw¡gh O;kid /jS l:iS lksbZ" (the sharp sickle, the clerk sits with a heavy heart). Explain in your own words what the "O;kid" (clerk) symbolizes in the context of the laborer's day.
questions.a: The clerk symbolizes the bureaucratic machinery that monitors and controls the laborer's work, reducing human effort to mere attendance and output. A wrong answer that treats the clerk as just a neutral observer shows the student misses the power dynamic: the clerk's "heavy heart" (लःस) implies complicity in exploitation.

questions.q: Using the prose background about Dhoomil, identify two supporting characters commonly found in his poems (other than the laborer) and state one line from the given poem that hints at their presence.
questions.a: The contractor (thekedar) and the clerk (munshi/O;kid) are recurring supporting characters. The line "lc ?kfV varfj rw¡gh O;kid /jS l:iS lksbZ" hints at the clerk; the contractor is implied in the wage negotiation ("cu iM+s rks lh/s&lh/s ugha rks njsjk nsdj" from the prose). A wrong answer that invents characters not in the text shows inability to connect prose context to poetic evidence.

questions.q: Compare the function of the "sharp sickle" (ck<+h dk"V) and the "clerk" (O;kid) in the poem. How do both serve as instruments of the system that exploits the laborer?
questions.a: The sickle is the tool of production that the laborer wields but does not own; the clerk is the tool of administration that records the laborer's output for the owner. Both are extensions of the exploitative system: one extracts physical labor, the other extracts surplus value. A wrong answer that treats the sickle as merely a farming tool misses the metaphorical equivalence Dhoomil draws between physical and bureaucratic violence.

questions.q: Critique the view that the supporting characters in Dhoomil's poem are flat stereotypes. Use evidence from the poem and the prose background to defend your judgment.
questions.a: They are not flat stereotypes but deliberate typifications: the clerk's "heavy heart" (लःस) suggests internal conflict, making him a complex cog in the machine. Dhoomil's prose says he portrays "ln~Hkko vkSj lekurk" (empathy and equality) even for oppressors. A wrong answer that calls them flat ignores the nuance Dhoomil builds through minimal detail.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza in the style of Dhoomil introducing a new supporting character—the "truck driver" who transports the harvested crop—showing his relationship to the laborer.
questions.a: A good stanza will use simple, rustic vocabulary, collective voice, and show the driver as another exploited worker or as an agent of the market. Example: "ट्रक वाला आया धूल उड़ाता / हमारी फसल ले जाता बाज़ार / उसका पसीना भी हमारे जैसा / पर मालिक उसका भी कोई और।" A poor answer will use literary Hindi, miss the collective perspective, or make the driver a villain without systemic context.
